name: Thymopentin

lead: Thymopentin is a five-amino-acid peptide based on the thymus hormone thymopoietin. It is classed as an immunostimulant and has been tested in HIV, atopic dermatitis, cancer and other immune-related conditions.
It appears in peptide and longevity discussion as an immune-modulating compound. No published trial has tested it for an appearance outcome.

paras: It is described as interacting with T cells, with binding to HLA-DR molecules reported in one study. Much recent work concerns delivery systems because peptides are poorly absorbed orally.
Safety information was not covered in the sources reviewed. Its regulatory status varies by country, and it is not an approved appearance treatment.

lead: Thymopentin (also abbreviated TP5) is a synthetic pentapeptide made of the amino acids arginine, lysine, aspartate, valine and tyrosine, derived from the thymus hormone thymopoietin. It is classed as an immunostimulant (ATC code L03AX09) and is described as interacting with T cells.[1]

Its place in appearance and longevity discussion is peripheral: it is mentioned as an immunomodulating peptide rather than a cosmetic agent. Published human research has concentrated on immune-related conditions, including early HIV-era studies, atopic dermatitis and cancer, and no trial of it for an appearance outcome was found.[1][2][3]

paras: Thymopentin is described as acting on T lymphocytes. The only mechanistic detail given in the encyclopedia entry is a 2007 study of its binding to HLA-DR molecules.[1] Because peptides are poorly absorbed when swallowed, a body of pharmaceutics research has examined carriers for delivering it, including lectin-conjugated PLGA nanoparticles for oral delivery and inhalable microparticles loaded with solid lipid nanoparticles for the lungs.[4][5][6]

A 1990 report in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology described thymopentin therapy in atopic dermatitis, with the title stating that it reduced clinical severity.[2] In the early AIDS era (roughly 1983 to 1985), several clinical studies tested it, and some patients showed short-term immune improvement under specific treatments.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a number of registered HIV-related studies of thymopentin (sold under the name Timunox in some registrations), including a phase 3 study in asymptomatic infected patients on antiretroviral therapy, and a phase 3 trial in patients after resection of small hepatocellular carcinoma whose status is recorded as unknown.[7][8][3] More recent investigations have covered rheumatoid arthritis, lung cancer, sepsis and infection prophylaxis in peritoneal dialysis.[1] No studies of thymopentin for skin appearance, ageing appearance or physique were found.
Current published work consists mostly of formulation and delivery research aimed at improving the stability and bioavailability of the peptide.[4][5][6]
